# Classical Supervised Learning {#sec-supervised}

::: {.chapter-goal}
#### In this chapter
You will train, tune and compare three classifiers, read which of your expensive predictor bands are actually doing work, combine the three into a majority vote, and clean the result without deleting the features you are trying to map.
:::

## What a classifier is doing

Strip away the algorithm names and supervised classification is one operation: given a table where each row is a location, the columns are measurements and one column is a label, learn a rule that predicts the label from the measurements, then apply that rule to every pixel in the image.

Everything in Chapters 8 to 14 existed to build the columns. Chapter 15 built the labels. This chapter is the shortest step in the chain and it gets the most attention, which is roughly the inverse of how much it matters.

## Three algorithms, three sets of blind spots

Earth Engine ships a fixed library of classifiers. Three cover nearly all remote sensing work, and the reason to know all three is not that one is best. It is that they fail differently, which is what makes the ensemble at the end of this chapter work.

**Random Forest** builds many decision trees. Each tree sees a bootstrap sample of the training data and, at each split, a random subset of the bands. The trees vote. Because the errors of individual trees are partly independent, averaging them cancels noise, which is why the method is so hard to overfit.

It is the right default for remote sensing for three specific reasons. It handles bands on wildly different scales without normalisation, and a feature stack containing reflectance from 0 to 1 alongside elevation in metres and backscatter in decibels is exactly that. It tolerates correlated predictors, and NDVI, EVI and SAVI are heavily correlated by construction. And it reports feature importance, which is the diagnostic in the next section.

Its real limitation shows up in regression rather than classification: a forest cannot predict a value outside the range it was trained on. Chapter 20 returns to this.

**Support vector machines** find the boundary that separates classes with the widest possible margin, in a space transformed by a kernel so that a boundary no straight line could draw becomes drawable. With a radial basis kernel, two parameters matter. `gamma` controls how local the boundary is, with high values producing a boundary that wraps tightly around individual training points and overfits. `cost` controls how much a misclassified training point is penalised, with high values also pushing towards overfitting.

SVM is distance based, and this has a consequence people trip over constantly. If one band ranges from 0 to 1 and another from 0 to 10,000, the second dominates the distance calculation entirely and the first is invisible to the model. This is precisely why Chapter 10 converted PALSAR digital numbers to gamma nought and divided Sentinel-2 by 10,000. That step was not tidiness. It was the difference between SVM working and SVM ignoring most of your stack.

**Gradient tree boosting** builds trees sequentially, each one fitting the errors the previous ones made. It is frequently the most accurate of the three on tabular data and the most willing to overfit noisy training data, because fitting the residuals of previous trees means eventually fitting the noise.

## Which bands are earning their place

`classifier.explain()` returns the internals of a trained model, including per band importance. On a stack built the hard way through Chapters 10 to 14, this chart answers a question worth real money: did the radar, texture and terrain bands justify the effort, or is NDVI doing all the work alone?

Read it in two directions.

**A band near zero is dead weight.** Drop it and retrain. If accuracy holds, the model just became cheaper to run, faster to export and more stable on new data. Feature reduction is one of the few free wins in this field.

**A band that dominates everything deserves suspicion, not satisfaction.** Ask whether it could be a disguised copy of the label. Chapter 22 works through a case where distance to the nearest competitor turned out to be exactly that, and produced a model reporting 100 percent accuracy that had learned nothing at all.

::: {.callout-tip}
## From the field
Feature importance is unreliable when predictors are strongly correlated. Random Forest spreads importance across a correlated group, so NDVI, EVI and SAVI may each look modestly useful when in fact one of them carries all the signal. Judge groups rather than individual bands, and confirm by dropping a group and retraining rather than trusting the chart alone.
:::

## Tuning, and knowing when to stop

Random Forest has few parameters that matter and the number of trees is the main one. Too few and the ensemble is unstable; past a point, accuracy plateaus and you are paying for computation.

The script sweeps tree counts and charts validation accuracy against them. Read the curve, do not just take the maximum. If accuracy is flat from 50 trees onward, the reported best value is noise and 50 is the honest choice: same accuracy, faster to run, faster to export.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Common failure: tuning against the wrong data
Building the error matrix from the training samples reports resubstitution accuracy, which measures how well the model memorised what it was shown. It is close to meaningless and always flattering. The validation set exists for this. Classify the validation features, then build the matrix from those.
:::

## The ensemble

Stack the three predictions as bands and take the per pixel mode. Where all three agree, nothing changes. Where they disagree, the majority wins and one model's idiosyncratic error is outvoted.

This works because the three algorithms fail differently. Ensembling three variants of the same algorithm gains almost nothing; the diversity is the mechanism, not the count.

There is a second, quieter benefit. The places where the three disagree form a map, and it is a better uncertainty product than most formal ones. A pixel that Random Forest calls mangrove, SVM calls other forest and gradient boosting calls mangrove is a pixel worth sending someone to look at. Chapter 17 uses this when deciding where to spend a limited field validation budget.

## Post processing without deleting your subject

The raw output of a pixel based classifier contains isolated misclassified pixels, the salt and pepper effect. A modal filter replaces each pixel with the most common value in its neighbourhood, consolidating small patches into their surroundings.

Be deliberate about the radius, because it is a minimum mapping unit decision wearing a disguise. A three pixel circle at 10 metre resolution erases any real feature smaller than roughly 30 metres across. Over a landscape of narrow fringing mangrove, that is entirely capable of deleting the thing you are mapping.

::: {.callout-important}
## Scientific integrity: smoothing changes your area figures
A modal filter applied before area calculation will systematically reduce the reported extent of any fragmented class and increase the extent of the dominant one. If you smooth, say so in the method description, and report whether the area statistic came from the smoothed or unsmoothed product. Two papers reporting different mangrove extents for the same delta have sometimes differed by nothing more than this.
:::

## Export rather than admire

Interactive display recomputes the entire chain on every pan and zoom. Over a full feature stack and a trained classifier, that is slow at best and hits the memory limit at worst.

Export the classification to an Asset, then load the finished asset for display and for everything downstream. It computes once. This single habit removes most of the timeout errors in Appendix B.

## Exercises {.unnumbered}

1. Toggle between the three individual classifications over a mangrove fringe. Where they disagree is where your map is genuinely uncertain. Save that disagreement layer; Chapter 17 uses it.
2. Deliberately sample before splitting instead of after, and record how much reported accuracy rises. That gap is the size of the lie.
3. Drop the three lowest importance bands and retrain. Report the accuracy change and decide whether they should stay.
4. Raise the focal mode radius to 6 pixels and find a real feature it deleted.
5. Set SVM `gamma` to 5 and rerun. Describe what overfitting looks like on a map, as distinct from what it looks like in a metric.
